n-m-e3-s1-01.title: How long was I in the pool? Where did it go wrong?
n-m-e3-s1-01.topic: Adding and subtracting time (subtracting time, when minutes cannot be subtracted)
n-m-e3-s1-01.goal: Use a clock to see why subtracting the smaller number from the larger number is wrong when the minutes cannot be subtracted, and then find the right answer by borrowing an hour and by counting up to the next o'clock.
n-m-e3-s1-01.material: Seoyun went into the pool at 3:50 and came out at 5:20. 1 hour is 60 minutes. To find how long Seoyun was in the pool, she calculated as follows.
n-m-e3-s1-01.thinking.0: Make your own cases where a calculation method goes wrong and check them
n-m-e3-s1-01.thinking.1: Compare two different ways of getting the same answer
n-m-e3-s1-01.thinking.2: Check the result of a calculation by looking back at the clock and estimating
n-m-e3-s1-01.prereq.1: Read the time on a clock
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line where Seoyun's calculation goes wrong.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s1.hint.0: Starting at 3:50 on the clock, first count how many minutes pass until 4 o'clock.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare Seoyun's answer, 2 hours 30 minutes, with the time the clock hands actually moved by adding one hour at a time to 3:50.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s1.line.0: Subtract the start time from the end time: 5:20 − 3:50.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s1.line.1: You cannot subtract 50 minutes from 20 minutes, so subtract the smaller number from the larger: 50 minutes − 20 minutes = 30 minutes.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s1.line.2: For the hours, 5 hours − 3 hours = 2 hours.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s1.line.3: So the time in the pool is 2 hours 30 minutes.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s1.explain: Line 1 is right. The difference between two times is found by subtracting the earlier time from the later time. The first mistake is in line 2. When you cannot subtract 50 minutes from 20 minutes, swapping the order of the subtraction makes the minutes between the times wrong. You need to borrow 1 hour from 5:20 and change it to 4:80. Then the minutes are 80−50=30 minutes and the hours are 4−3=1 hour, so it is 1 hour 30 minutes. Lines 3 and 4 are wrong because they carry over the mistake in line 2.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.prompt: Make two different cases where Seoyun's method gives an answer different from the correct one. Choose a start time and an end time so that the hour of the end time is greater and the minutes of the end time are less than the minutes of the start time. Use only times from 1 o'clock to 11 o'clock.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.hint.0: First choose two times so that the minutes of the end time are less than the minutes of the start time.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the value you get with Seoyun's method and the value you get by counting on the clock, and see whether they are different.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The hours of the start and end are between 1 and 11.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use a natural number from 1 to 11 for the hour.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.fail.c2: Please use a natural number from 0 to 59 for the minutes.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.ok.c3: The hour of the end time is greater.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The hour of the end time must be greater than the hour of the start time.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.ok.c4: The minutes of the end time are less, so you cannot subtract directly. Seoyun's method is wrong in this case.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.fail.c4: The minutes of the end time must be less than the minutes of the start time.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s2.explain: For example, from 2:45 to 4:10, Seoyun's method gives 2 hours 35 minutes, but counting on the clock gives 1 hour 25 minutes. You have to borrow an hour only when the minutes of the end time are less, so the method goes wrong in this kind of case. When the minutes are greater or equal, Seoyun's method is right.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.prompt: Choose all the ways that correctly find the time from 3:50 to 5:20.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.hint.0: Work out the time each method actually gives, and compare it with the time you count on the clock hands.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.hint.1: For each method, look for whether it includes the minutes from 3:50 to 4:00.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.o.a: Subtract the smaller number from the larger for the minutes, and subtract the hours too
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.r.a: If you subtract the smaller number from the larger one of 20 and 50 minutes, the minutes between the two times come out wrong. Count how many minutes it is from 3:50 to 4 o'clock.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.o.b: Split it into 3:50 to 4:00, 4:00 to 5:00, and 5:00 to 5:20, and add them
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.r.b: That is correct thinking. If you find each part and add them, it matches the time counted on the clock.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.o.c: The hour hand went from 3 to 5, so it is 2 hours, and you ignore the minute hand
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.r.c: The minutes the minute hand points to also count toward the time. Look again at where the minute hand is at 3:50 and at 5:20.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.o.d: Change 5:20 to 4:80 and subtract the hours and the minutes separately
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.r.d: That is correct thinking. If you borrow 1 hour and change it to 60 minutes, you can subtract the minutes.
n-m-e3-s1-01.s.s3.explain: Both methods give 1 hour 30 minutes. One adds up the time by breaking it at o'clock times, and the other borrows 1 hour and changes it to 60 minutes. When you cannot subtract the minutes, you do not subtract the smaller number from the larger; you borrow an hour.

n-m-e3-s1-02.title: Finding the times when the clock hands make a right angle
n-m-e3-s1-02.topic: Plane figures (angles and right angles, the angle made by clock hands)
n-m-e3-s1-02.goal: Find and check for yourself the o'clock times when the two hands of a clock make a right angle, and say, using the number of number-spaces, that a right angle is one equal part of a full turn of the clock.
n-m-e3-s1-02.material: A clock has 12 numbers placed in a circle. At an o'clock time, the long hand points to 12 and the short hand points to the hour. If you put the corner of a right-angle triangle ruler or a square piece of paper at the center of the clock, you can tell whether it is a right angle. At 3 o'clock, the two hands make a right angle.
n-m-e3-s1-02.thinking.0: Test the cases that fit the condition with a right-angle triangle ruler
n-m-e3-s1-02.thinking.1: Check the cases one by one and find all the possible ones
n-m-e3-s1-02.thinking.2: Express the size of an angle as a part of a full turn
n-m-e3-s1-02.prereq.0: Read o'clock times on a clock
n-m-e3-s1-02.prereq.1: Know the meaning of a right angle and use a right-angle triangle ruler
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.prompt: At 3 o'clock, if you put the corner of a right-angle triangle ruler at the center of the clock, it fits the two hands exactly. At 1 o'clock, how does the angle made by the two hands compare with a right angle?
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.hint.0: Point with your finger to the space between 12 and 1 and the space between 12 and 3 on the clock.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.hint.1: Put a right-angle triangle ruler (or the corner of a square) on the paper and compare the space between the hands at 3 o'clock with the space between the hands at 1 o'clock.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.o.a: It is bigger than a right angle
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.r.a: At 1 o'clock, the hour hand has moved only a very little from 12. Compare it with the space between the hands at 3 o'clock.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.o.b: It is equal to a right angle
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.r.b: Compare whether the opening between the hour hand and the minute hand is the same as at 3 o'clock.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.o.c: It is smaller than a right angle
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.r.c: The space between the hands is narrower than at 3 o'clock. You can check it by putting a right-angle triangle ruler on it.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.o.d: The hands overlap, so there is no angle
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.r.d: At 1 o'clock, the two hands do not overlap. Look again at the number the hour hand points to.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s1.explain: At 1 o'clock, the hour hand points to 1 and the minute hand points to 12. The space between the two hands is narrower than at 3 o'clock, so the angle is smaller than a right angle.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s2.prompt: At an o'clock time, the minute hand (long hand) points to 12. Write h for the number the hour hand (short hand) points to, and find and write the o'clock times when the two hands make a right angle. Enter different times.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s2.hint.0: Keeping the minute hand at 12, move the hour hand one by one from 1 o'clock to 12 o'clock and put a right-angle triangle ruler on each.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s2.hint.1: Count how many spaces away from 12 the hour hand is when it makes a right angle.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s2.var.h: The number the hour hand points to (1~12)
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s2.ok.c1: It is a number from 1 to 12.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use a natural number from 1 to 12 for h.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The two hands make a right angle.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s2.fail.c2: At this time, the two hands do not make a right angle. Put a right-angle triangle ruler on the clock.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s2.explain: The two hands make a right angle at 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock. At 6 o'clock, the two hands stretch out in a straight line, which is bigger than a right angle, and at 12 o'clock, the two hands overlap.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s3.prompt: Count the number-spaces from 12 to the hour hand. Write the number of spaces for the times that make a right angle, and explain, connecting it to a full turn of the clock, why that number of spaces makes a right angle.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s3.hint.0: At 3 o'clock, point with your finger from 12 to 3 and count how many spaces it is.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s3.hint.1: Count how many spaces in all it takes to go around the clock once, and think about how many right angles together make a full turn.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. A right-angle time is when the hour hand is ... from 12
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you count the number of spaces from 12 to the hour hand exactly?
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect it to how many spaces a full turn of the clock has?
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Can you also say, using the number of spaces, why 6 o'clock or 1 o'clock is not a right angle?
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s3.model.0: A right angle is 3 spaces away from 12. A full turn of the clock is 12 spaces, and 4 right angles make a full turn, so 12 divided by 4 is 3 spaces.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s3.model.1: At 3 o'clock and 9 o'clock, the number is 3 spaces away from 12. 3 spaces is one fourth of the 12 spaces in a full turn, so it is a right angle.
n-m-e3-s1-02.s.s3.model.2: If you divide 12 spaces into 4 equal parts, each part is 3 spaces. So if it is 3 spaces away from 12, it is a right angle.

n-m-e3-s1-03.title: Is division also the same when you swap the order, like multiplication?
n-m-e3-s1-03.topic: Division (sharing equally, the relationship between multiplication and division)
n-m-e3-s1-03.goal: Check by making equations yourself whether what is true for multiplication is also true for division, and explain with an example that if you swap the numbers in a division, the value is not the same.
n-m-e3-s1-03.material: Sua said this: "3×8=24 and 8×3=24. In multiplication you get the same answer when you swap the order. So division will be the same when you swap the order too." Division 12÷3 means 12 things shared equally among 3 people.
n-m-e3-s1-03.thinking.0: Decide whether a property that is true in one area can be carried over as it is to another area
n-m-e3-s1-03.thinking.1: Test a statement by making a counterexample yourself
n-m-e3-s1-03.thinking.2: Explain to a friend using an example
n-m-e3-s1-03.prereq.1: Know that division means sharing equally
n-m-e3-s1-03.prereq.2: In multiplication, the product is the same when you swap the order
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.prompt: We want to find out whether what Sua said is right. What would be a good way?
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.hint.0: Is what Sua said about multiplication or division? First decide what you should examine.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.hint.1: Choose one division equation, swap the first number and the second number, and write both equations.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.o.a: Write more multiplication equations, and if they are all the same, say division is the same too
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.r.a: Division is connected to multiplication, so I believe swapping the order gives the same answer
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.o.b: Whether swapping the order gives the same answer in multiplication has to be looked at separately from whether it does in division.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.r.b: You cannot decide that the order in division is the same just because it is connected to multiplication. Calculate it yourself.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.o.c: Choose one division equation, calculate it with the order swapped, and compare the two results
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.o.d: Check again the 3×8=24 and 8×3=24 that Sua wrote
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.r.d: You already know the multiplication equations are right. What you have to examine is division.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s1.explain: What Sua said carries over a statement from multiplication to division. Being true for multiplication does not tell you whether it is true for division, so you need to choose one division equation and calculate it with the order swapped.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.prompt: Make three different division equations where what Sua said is wrong. a÷b must share out equally with nothing left over, and b÷a, with the order swapped, must not share out with nothing left over. b is 2 or more, and a is a number 100 or less.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.hint.0: Think of one equation you know from the multiplication table, rewrite it as a division equation, and also write the equation with the first and second numbers swapped next to it.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.hint.1: Draw the swapped equation as sharing marbles. Check how many marbles each person gets.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.ok.c1: a is a natural number 100 or less.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use a natural number from 1 to 100 for a.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.ok.c2: b is a natural number 2 or more.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Please use a natural number 2 or more for b.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.ok.c3: a÷b divides with nothing left over.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.fail.c3: a÷b must divide with nothing left over. Choose an equation with no remainder.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.ok.c4: b÷a, with the order swapped, does not divide with nothing left over.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.fail.c4: If b÷a also divides with nothing left over, it is a case where Sua is right. Choose numbers that do not divide when you swap the order.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s2.explain: For example, 12÷3=4 works, but with 3÷12, you cannot share 3 things equally among 12 people. Unlike multiplication, division does not give the same value when you swap the order. The only exception is when the first and second numbers are the same (like 6÷6).
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.prompt: How would you tell Sua? Use one equation you just made to write why you must not swap the order in division.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.hint.0: Take one equation you made above as it is and write the swapped equation next to it.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.hint.1: Describe the two equations as sharing marbles. Write down which one divides with nothing left over.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you do both calculations of the equation I wrote exactly?
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write clearly which one divides and which one does not?
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say that multiplication and division are different?
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.model.0: Sua, 12÷3 is 4, but with 3÷12 you cannot share 3 things equally among 12 people. In division you must not swap the order.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.model.1: 24÷6=4. But 6÷24 does not divide. Unlike multiplication, in division the result changes when the first and second numbers are swapped.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.model.2: 18÷2 is 9, but 2÷18 cannot be shared out with nothing left over. So swapping the order does not give the same answer.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.model.3: Sua, 12÷3=4, but 3÷12 cannot be calculated. So no.
n-m-e3-s1-03.s.s3.model.4: Sua, 12÷3=4, but 3÷12 has no answer. If you swap the order, it changes.

n-m-e3-s1-04.title: Can we load 3 boxes onto the truck by estimating?
n-m-e3-s1-04.topic: Addition and subtraction (estimating three-digit numbers, estimated value and actual value)
n-m-e3-s1-04.goal: When checking whether a limit is exceeded, learn from new information that a value rounded down is smaller than the actual value and cannot be trusted, and make and explain a case where the estimate is wrong.
n-m-e3-s1-04.material: One truck can carry up to 700 kg. We want to load 3 boxes. Haram wants to estimate the numbers to see whether they can be loaded. Each time new information comes out, choose what you think.
n-m-e3-s1-04.thinking.0: Look at the direction in which the difference between the estimate and the actual value builds up
n-m-e3-s1-04.thinking.1: Change your judgment according to new information
n-m-e3-s1-04.thinking.2: Make cases where the estimate is wrong yourself
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.prompt: Each time new information comes out, choose how your thinking changes.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first compare whether Haram's estimate is bigger or smaller than the actual weight.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write the estimated numbers next to the actual numbers and count how many times the difference builds up.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.0.info: The truck can carry up to 700 kg. We want to load 3 boxes, and each box weighs 249 kg. Haram estimated 249 as the nearest hundred, 200, and said 200+200+200=600. 600 is less than 700.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: Haram says the 3 boxes can be loaded. What do you think of this estimate?
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.0.after: When 249 is reduced to 200, 49 kg is lost from each box. With 3 boxes, the lost amount builds up 3 times, so the actual weight is more than 600.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: I believe 600 is less than 700, so the 3 boxes can be loaded
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is thinking that uses the estimated value as if it were the actual weight. Look at how much disappeared when it was changed to 200.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Estimates can't be trusted, so I should not estimate and should only use exact numbers
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Estimates are useful too. What matters is looking at which estimate fits which question.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Since it was rounded down to 200, the actual weight could be greater, so we need to find out more
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Estimating by rounding down to 200 can be trusted just the same however many boxes there are
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The more boxes there are, the more times the lost amount builds up. Count how much builds up when there are 3 boxes.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Haram also tried estimating by rounding 249 up to the nearest hundred, 300. 300+300+300=900. 900 is more than 700.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now, what can we say about the actual weight?
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.1.after: The value 600, estimated by rounding down, is less than the actual weight, and the value 900, estimated by rounding up, is more than the actual weight. So the actual weight is between the two values. 700 is between them, so it is hard to decide by estimating alone.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The actual weight is more than 600 and less than 900, so it still cannot be compared with 700
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: 900 is more than 700, so we can say it can't be loaded
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: The value estimated by rounding up is larger than the actual one. Look at whether 900 being more than 700 alone means the actual weight is also more.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 750, exactly in the middle of the two estimates, is the actual weight
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: There is no basis for saying the middle of the two estimated values is the actual value.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: The first estimate, 600, is correct, so we can say it can be loaded
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Look again at the fact that the estimate rounded down to 200 was less than the actual weight.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: Can these 3 boxes be loaded onto a truck that can carry up to 700 kg? And what did you learn from this?
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.2.after: 747 is more than 700, so they can't be loaded. When checking whether a limit is exceeded, do not feel safe because a value estimated by rounding down is at or below the limit. It is safe only when the value estimated by rounding up is at or below the limit, and if it is unclear, add exactly.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: They can be loaded. If the sum estimated by rounding down is at or below the limit, they can always be loaded
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The value 600 estimated by rounding down was 700 or less, but the actual 747 is more than 700.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: They can't be loaded. If it is hard to tell by estimating, you can add exactly
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: They can be loaded. The value 900 estimated by rounding up is close to 700, so it is fine
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.2.r.c: 747 is more than 700, so they can't be loaded. Regardless of the estimate being close, you must compare using the actual value.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: They can't be loaded. If the sum estimated by rounding up is at or below the limit it is safe, but this time estimating alone could not tell us
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s1.reflect: At first it was easy to trust the estimated 600, but it changes once you know that a value estimated by rounding down is less than the actual one. Looking at it together with the value estimated by rounding up, we could see the range the actual value is in. Say at which step your thinking changed and what changed it.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s2.prompt: Make the weights of three boxes so that Haram's first estimating method (rounding each box down to the nearest hundred and adding) gives 700 or less, but adding exactly gives more than 700. Each box is 100 kg or more and 399 kg or less. Make two different sets.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s2.hint.0: Choose numbers whose tens digit and ones digit are large for each box's weight. Count how much is lost each time you round down.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s2.hint.1: Calculate the value of the three numbers rounded down to the hundreds and added, and the value added as they are, and compare each with 700.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s2.ok.c1: All three boxes are 100 kg or more and 399 kg or less.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use natural numbers from 100 to 399 for the weights of the three boxes.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum estimated by rounding down is 700 or less, so Haram would say they can be loaded.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Make the sum estimated by rounding down (each rounded down to the hundreds and added) 700 or less.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s2.ok.c3: Added exactly, it is more than 700, so they can't be loaded.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The exact sum must be more than 700 for the estimate to be wrong.
n-m-e3-s1-04.s.s2.explain: If you round each box down to the hundreds, up to 99 kg is lost from each box. With three boxes, up to 297 kg can be lost, so even if the estimated sum is 700 or less, the actual sum can be more than 700.

n-m-e3-s1-05.title: Saying the length of a pencil in cm and mm
n-m-e3-s1-05.topic: Length and time (the relationship between cm and mm, the unit mm)
n-m-e3-s1-05.goal: Use the relationship between cm and mm to show the same length in two ways, and understand why the mm part cannot be 10 or more and why the smaller the unit, the bigger the number.
n-m-e3-s1-05.material: Jiu measured the length of a pencil with a ruler. 1 cm is 10 mm. 4 cm 7 mm is the same length as 47 mm. A length can be said as "_ cm _ mm" or as "_ mm".
n-m-e3-s1-05.thinking.0: Show the same amount in a different unit
n-m-e3-s1-05.thinking.1: Check the rule for writing numbers (mm is less than 10)
n-m-e3-s1-05.thinking.2: Connect the size of a unit with the size of a number
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s1.prompt: A friend wrote the length of a pencil as 6 cm 13 mm. 1 cm is 10 mm. How should this length be rewritten most appropriately?
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s1.hint.0: Change 6 cm to mm and add 13 mm.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s1.hint.1: Group the mm you get into 10 mm groups and split it into cm and the remaining mm.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s1.r.a: 6 cm is 60 mm. Compare it with the number made by putting 6 cm 13 mm side by side.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s1.r.b: It is the sum of 6 and 13. cm and mm are different units, so you cannot add them as they are.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s1.r.d: When 10 mm out of 13 mm becomes 1 cm, the cm goes up by one, but in this answer the cm stays the same.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s1.explain: 6 cm is 60 mm, and 60+13=73 mm. Grouping 73 mm into 10 mm groups gives 7 cm 3 mm. If mm is 10 or more, change it to 1 cm and add it to the cm.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s2.prompt: Choose the lengths of three pencils of your own and write them. Each length is 10 cm or more and 19 cm or less, and the mm in "_ cm _ mm" is a number from 1 to 9. Also write the same length in mm only. Make three different lengths.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s2.hint.0: First decide the length of the pencil as "_ cm _ mm". The number on the mm side must be less than 10.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s2.hint.1: To change the cm number to mm, think about how many groups of how many mm there are, and add the remaining mm.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s2.var.c: The same length in mm only
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use a natural number from 10 to 19 for cm.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Please use a natural number from 1 to 9 for mm.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The length written only in mm is equal to the cm and mm lengths put together.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The length written only in mm is not the same length as "_ cm _ mm". Change the cm to mm and add.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s2.explain: 1 cm is 10 mm, so a cm is a×10 mm. If you add the mm to that, you get the length written only in mm. Even for the same length, the number is much bigger when you write it in mm.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.prompt: Compare the number for the same pencil length written in cm and written in mm. Which number is bigger, and why?
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.hint.0: Choose one of the lengths you just made and write the number in cm (the cm part of "_ cm _ mm") and the number in mm side by side.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.hint.1: Check with a ruler how many mm fit in 1 cm, and connect the size of the unit with the number.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.o.a: The number in cm is bigger, because cm is the bigger unit
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.r.a: If you measure with a bigger unit, the number gets smaller even for the same length. Compare the two numbers for the length you just made.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.o.b: The two numbers are the same, because the length is the same
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.r.b: The length is the same, but the units are different, so the numbers are different. Compare the two numbers for the length you made.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.o.c: The number in mm is bigger, because mm is the smaller unit so you need more of them
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.o.d: It depends on the length. Sometimes cm is bigger
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.r.d: 1 cm is always 10 mm, so for any length the number in mm is bigger.
n-m-e3-s1-05.s.s3.explain: There are 10 mm in 1 cm, so if you measure the same length in mm, the number becomes nearly 10 times bigger. If you measure with a small unit, the number gets bigger, and if you measure with a big unit, the number gets smaller.

n-m-e3-s2-01.title: Looking at how Hajun counted the chairs in the gym, step by step
n-m-e3-s2-01.topic: Multiplication ((two-digit number)×(two-digit number)): place value of partial products when splitting the multiplier
n-m-e3-s2-01.goal: When multiplying (two-digit number)×(two-digit number) by splitting the multiplier into tens and ones, check line by line whether the place value of each partial product is right, and check the answer with estimating and the last digit.
n-m-e3-s2-01.material: In the gym, chairs were put out 34 to a row in 27 rows. To find how many chairs there are in all, Hajun split 27 into 20 and 7 and multiplied. Below is the calculation Hajun wrote.
n-m-e3-s2-01.thinking.0: Find where the calculation first goes wrong
n-m-e3-s2-01.thinking.1: Check whether the answer is right using estimating and the last digit
n-m-e3-s2-01.thinking.2: Say the value (so many tens) that the digit in the tens place stands for
n-m-e3-s2-01.prereq.1: Know that multiplying by a number of tens makes the product ten times the product of that number (tens × ones)
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s1.prompt: Read the lines Hajun calculated from the top. Which line is the first one that is wrong?
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s1.hint.0: For each line, do that line's calculation again yourself and compare it with the value Hajun wrote.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s1.hint.1: Go back to the story that there are 34 chairs in each row, and say in words, line by line, how many rows are being multiplied.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s1.line.0: Split 27 into 20 and 7 and multiply separately.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s1.line.3: 238+68=306, so there are 306 chairs in all.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the first one that is wrong. The 2 in 27 is the digit in the tens place, so it means 20, not 2. 34×20 is 680, which is ten times 34×2=68. So 238+680=918, and there are 918 chairs. The sum in line 4, 238+68=306, is right as a calculation, but it follows from the wrong 68. Lines 1 and 2 are right.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the ways to find out that 306 is a wrong answer without calculating 34×27 again.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s2.hint.0: Think about roughly how big the answer should be by changing 34 and 27 to similar easy numbers.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s2.hint.1: Test with small multiplication examples which digits you multiply to decide the last digit of a product.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s2.o.a: A product only has to be greater than the number being multiplied, 34, so I only need to see whether 306 is greater than 34
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s2.r.a: You only checked that it is greater than 34. Estimate about how much 34 taken 27 times should be.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s2.o.b: If I estimate 34 as 30 and 27 as 30, it should be about 900, and 306 is much smaller
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s2.o.c: If I add the ones digits, 4+7=11, so the ones digit of the product should be 1
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s2.r.c: In multiplication, you multiply the ones digits, not add them. Look at the number you get by multiplying 4 and 7.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s2.o.d: If I multiply the ones digits, 4×7=28, so the ones digit of the product should be 8
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s2.explain: 34×27 is about 30×30=900, and from 28, which is the ones digits 4 and 7 multiplied, the last digit should be 8. 306 is far from about 900 and its last digit is 6, so it is a wrong answer. Estimating and checking the last digit can be used when judging whether a calculation is right.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.prompt: Hajun calculated 34×20 as 34×2=68. Why should this value be 680?
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.hint.0: Draw the splitting of 27 into 20 and 7 as 20 rows and 7 rows with 34 in each, and compare how many times 2 rows 20 rows is.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write side by side what the multiplier means when you calculate 34×7 and when you calculate 34×20, and compare them.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.o.a: Because the 3 in 34 is the digit in the tens place, so you have to multiply it as 30
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.r.a: Splitting 34 into 30 and 4 is also possible, but it is a different matter from Hajun's mistake. Look at which number was multiplied when 27 was split.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.o.b: Because to line it up with 238, you have to put a 2 in front of 68
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.r.b: Putting a digit in front of 68 does not make the multiplied value right. Think about how many times 20 is 2.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.o.c: Because the 2 in 27 is the digit in the tens place, so you have to multiply by 20
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.o.d: Because when you multiply two-digit numbers, you always have to put one 0 at the end of the product
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.r.d: This is thinking that memorized a rule without knowing why the 0 is put on. You did not put a 0 on when you multiplied by 7, so think about why it is different.
n-m-e3-s2-01.s.s3.explain: 27 is the sum of 20 and 7. 20 is ten times 2, so 34×20 is 680, which is ten times 34×2. You did not put a 0 on when you multiplied by 7, so the statement "always put a 0 on" is wrong.

n-m-e3-s2-02.title: How many rectangles can you make with 360 tiles?
n-m-e3-s2-02.topic: Multiplication ((two-digit number)×(two-digit number)): several multiplication equations with the same product
n-m-e3-s2-02.goal: Using the fact that when you multiply one number by some times and make the other number that fraction of itself, the product stays the same, make and check several (two-digit number)×(two-digit number) equations whose product is 360.
n-m-e3-s2-02.material: There are 360 tiles. You want to lay these tiles in a rectangle with no gaps, with the same number in each horizontal row. Jiyun said you can lay them 12 to a row in 30 rows. Other friends said there are other ways too.
n-m-e3-s2-02.thinking.0: Find several pairs with the same product
n-m-e3-s2-02.thinking.1: Find the rule for how the other number changes when one number gets bigger
n-m-e3-s2-02.thinking.2: Tell adding and subtracting apart from multiplying and dividing
n-m-e3-s2-02.prereq.1: The relationship between multiplication and division
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s1.prompt: 12×30=360. Choose all the multiplication equations whose product stays 360.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate each equation yourself and compare it with 360.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s1.hint.1: Compared with 12×30, write down which number became how many times bigger, or how much it increased or decreased.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s1.r.b: Only one number was doubled. Calculate whether the product was also doubled.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s1.r.d: 2 was added to one number and 2 was subtracted from the other. Calculate to check whether the product stays the same if you subtract as much as you add.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s1.explain: If you double 12 and halve 30, it is 24×15, and if you halve 12 and double 30, it is 6×60. Both are 360. 24×30 is 720 and 14×28 is 392.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s2.prompt: You want to lay 360 tiles in a rectangle with no gaps. When you lay a tiles in each horizontal row in b rows, find 3 different ways in which a and b are both two-digit numbers. Count ones that only swap the horizontal and vertical as the same way.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s2.hint.0: Think about whether 360 can be made as a product of two equal numbers, and first put an easy number like 10 or 20 in for a and find b.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s2.hint.1: After you decide a, find b, and check that both are two-digit numbers.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s2.var.a: Number of tiles in a row, a (two-digit number)
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use a natural number from 10 to 99 for a.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Please use a natural number from 10 to 99 for b.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s2.explain: The pairs of two-digit numbers that multiply to 360 are 10×36, 12×30, 15×24, and 18×20. As the first number gets bigger, the second number gets smaller.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s3.prompt: 18×20=360. If you increase the number of tiles in a row 3 times, from 20 to 60, how many rows should the 18 rows become for the product to stay 360?
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s3.hint.0: Group 360 into groups of 60 and count how many rows all 360 tiles make when 60 are put in each row.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s3.hint.1: Draw the tiles that were laid 20 to a row in 18 rows being laid out again 60 to a row.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s3.r.a: The number of tiles in a row became 3 times as many, so you also increased the number of rows 3 times. Calculate how many tiles that makes in all.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s3.r.c: You reduced the number of rows by only 3, as much as the 40 tiles added to each row. Calculate whether the 40 added tiles can be traded for 3 rows.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s3.r.d: If the number of tiles in a row increased but the number of rows stays the same, think about what happens to the total number of tiles.
n-m-e3-s2-02.s.s3.explain: 60×6=360. If you make one number 3 times as big, for the product to stay the same the other number must become one third (18÷3=6). With 54 rows, 60×54=3240.

n-m-e3-s2-03.title: If the check is right, is Seoyun's answer always right too?
n-m-e3-s2-03.topic: Division (division with a remainder): quotient and remainder, checking
n-m-e3-s2-03.goal: In a division with a remainder, make a counterexample showing that even if the check equation is right, the answer can be wrong when the remainder is not less than the divisor, and explain the reason in writing.
n-m-e3-s2-03.material: Seoyun wants to share 50 candies equally among 6 people. Seoyun took away 6 seven times, which is 42 candies, and 50−42=8, so she said she gives each person 7 candies and 8 are left over. Seoyun said that 6×7+8=50, so the check is right and the answer is right too.
n-m-e3-s2-03.thinking.0: Judge whether the check is enough
n-m-e3-s2-03.thinking.1: Make a counterexample where the check equation is right but the answer is wrong
n-m-e3-s2-03.thinking.2: Explain the condition that the remainder is less than the divisor
n-m-e3-s2-03.prereq.0: Find the quotient and remainder of a division
n-m-e3-s2-03.prereq.1: Check using the relationship between multiplication and division
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.prompt: Seoyun said, "The check is right, so the answer is right too." What do you think of this?
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.hint.0: Draw in a picture the candies left after Seoyun gave out 7 each. See whether there is anything more that can be done with those candies.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.hint.1: Apart from the check equation, think while sharing candies about what the leftover candies must be like for the division to be finished.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.o.a: It is right. 6×7+8 is 50, so the quotient 7 and the remainder 8 are the right answer
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.r.a: This thinking only looked at whether the check equation equals the number being divided, 50. Share candies yourself and examine whether the answer to a division has any other conditions it must meet.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.o.b: It is wrong. The 6 people can each get one more of the 8 leftover
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.o.c: It is wrong. 6×7 is 42, not 50, so the check equation is wrong
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.r.c: 6×7=42 is right. Check again that adding the remainder 8 to 42 makes 50.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.o.d: I can't tell. I won't know unless I actually share the candies one by one
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.r.d: Compare the number of leftover candies with the number of people to see if there is a clue you can use without actually sharing the candies.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s1.explain: 6×7+8=50 is right, but there are 8 candies left over and only 6 people, so each can get one more. The sharing is not finished yet. Even if the check equation is right, you also have to look at whether the remainder is less than the divisor, 6.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 pairs of quotient and remainder like Seoyun's where the check equation 6×(quotient)+(remainder)=50 is right but they are wrong as the answer to the division. They must be different pairs, not Seoyun's answer (quotient 7, remainder 8). The quotient and remainder are natural numbers 1 or more.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s2.hint.0: Choose the quotient first, and find the remainder by subtracting the value multiplied by 6 from 50.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s2.hint.1: Check whether the candies for the remainder you found can be shared among the 6 people one more time.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The quotient and remainder are natural numbers 1 or more.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s2.fail.c1: Please use natural numbers 1 or more for the quotient and remainder.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s2.ok.c3: The remainder is 6 or more, so it is wrong as the answer to the division.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s2.fail.c3: In this pair the remainder is less than 6, so it is a correct answer to the division. Please find a wrong answer.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s2.ok.c4: It is a different pair from Seoyun's answer.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s2.fail.c4: Quotient 7 and remainder 8 is Seoyun's answer. Please find a different pair.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s2.explain: If the quotient is less than 8, the remainder that makes 6×(quotient)+(remainder)=50 is always greater than 6. Like quotient 6 with remainder 14, or quotient 5 with remainder 20, even if the check equation is right, you can still share more. Seoyun's quotient 7 and remainder 8 is such a case too. The correct answer is only quotient 8 and remainder 2.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.prompt: Tell Seoyun the correct quotient and remainder, and write the reason why the remainder cannot be 8.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.hint.0: Count again how many candies each of the 6 people can get out of 50, and find how many candies are left over.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the number of leftover candies with the number of people, 6, and write in words whether the leftover candies can be shared further.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. Seoyun, the quotient is ..., and the remainder is ...
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write both the correct quotient and the remainder?
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain why the remainder must be less than 6, using the story of sharing candy?
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you word it so that Seoyun won't feel bad?
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.model.0: The quotient is 8 and the remainder is 2. If the remainder were 8, which is more than 6, you could give each person 1 more, so giving 7 each is not finished yet.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.model.1: If you give each person 8 candies, 2 are left over. The leftover has to be less than 6, but if 8 were left you could share again, so Seoyun's answer is wrong.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: Used both "must be less than 6" and "can share again."
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.model.2: 6×8=48 and 50−48=2, so the quotient is 8 and the remainder is 2. The remainder must be less than the divisor 6. If 6 or more is left, you can give out one more round.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.model.3: Seoyun, if you make the quotient 8, the remainder is 2. If the remainder is 6 or more, you can still divide more, so the remainder can only be a number less than 6.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.model.4: The quotient is 8 and the remainder is 2. A remainder of 8 is greater than the divisor 6, so it can't be.
n-m-e3-s2-03.s.s3.model.5: The quotient is 8 and the remainder is 2. The remainder can't be greater than 6.

n-m-e3-s2-04.title: How do you draw the longest line segment inside a circle?
n-m-e3-s2-04.topic: Circle (radius, diameter): the longest line segment in a circle is the diameter
n-m-e3-s2-04.goal: Measure the lengths of line segments joining two points on a circle, guess what kind of segment is the longest, and use the fact that a segment through the center is twice the radius as the reason, applying it to another circle.
n-m-e3-s2-04.material: There is a circular piece of paper with a radius of 5 cm. Sea wants to find out which kind of segment is the longest among the straight segments joining two points on the circle.
n-m-e3-s2-04.thinking.0: Doubting a conclusion drawn from little data
n-m-e3-s2-04.thinking.1: Finding and testing the kind of case that is missing
n-m-e3-s2-04.thinking.2: Knowing the reason and applying it to other numbers
n-m-e3-s2-04.prereq.0: Knowing the center, radius, and diameter of a circle
n-m-e3-s2-04.prereq.1: Measuring lengths in cm and adding them
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose how your thinking changes each time new information comes in.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write down the lengths of the segments measured so far, and look for a kind that has not been measured yet.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the new information makes your thinking firmer or shakes it, and at the step where a reason appears, think about whether that reason also works for other numbers.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.info: There is a circular piece of paper with a radius of 5 cm. Sea measured three straight segments joining two points on the circle and got 6 cm, 8 cm, and 9 cm. None of the three segments passed through the middle point (the center) of the circle.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think the longest segment you can draw inside a circle is like?
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.after: It is too early to decide the longest from measuring just three. You need to check whether there are kinds of segments that haven't been measured yet.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The longest one measured, 9 cm, will be the longest segment in the circle.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You decided it was the longest after measuring only three. Look back and check whether any segment not yet measured is longer.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Any segment drawn inside a circle will have the same length.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.r.b: Sea's 6 cm, 8 cm, and 9 cm are different from each other. This idea doesn't fit them.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.o.c: There might be a segment longer than 9 cm, so I want to measure other segments too.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.r.c: This is a thought that doubts whether the measurements represent all segments and wants to test more.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.o.d: I haven't measured a segment through the center yet, so I want to measure that too.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a thought that looks for a missing case and wants to test it.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.1.info: Sea measured three segments through the center and all were 10 cm. She measured seven more segments not through the center, and all were shorter than 10 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.1.after: With ten results you can make a guess. But you still don't know why the segment through the center is the longest. Let's look for the reason.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.1.o.a: A segment through the center must be 5 cm, the same as the radius.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The length from the center to a point on the circle is 5 cm. Look at how many times this length is repeated in a segment through the center.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.1.o.b: I think the segments through the center are the longest and are all 10 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You made a guess from the measurements and checked whether there was an example that contradicts it.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.1.o.c: If you draw more segments, some will be longer than 10 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The number of segments has nothing to do with the length. Even after measuring seven more, none went over 10 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.1.o.d: I only measured ten, so it is still too early to decide it is the longest.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You make a guess but, not knowing the reason yet, hold off on being sure.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.2.info: Sea found the reason. The distance from the center to any point on the circle is always 5 cm. A segment through the center is two 5 cm lengths joined, so it is 10 cm. For a segment not through the center with endpoints A and B, the way from A through the center back to B is 5+5=10 cm, and going straight from A to B is shorter than that.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.2.ask: In another circle with a radius of 6 cm, how many cm is the longest segment?
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.2.after: Whatever the radius is, the longest segment is the radius repeated twice. If the radius is 6 cm, it is 12 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.2.o.a: 6 cm, because the distance from the center to a point on the circle is the longest
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.2.r.a: The radius of 6 cm is the length from the center to one end. Think about how long it becomes if you go through the center to the opposite end.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.2.o.b: 11 cm, because the radius grew by 1 cm, so the longest segment also grew by 1 cm
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.2.r.b: If the radius grows by 1 cm, both sides of the center grow by 1 cm each. Calculate how many cm it grows from the 10 cm it was when the radius was 5 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.2.o.c: 12 cm, because it is two 6 cm lengths joined
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.2.o.d: 10 cm, because even if the circle is different, the longest segment is the same
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.st.2.r.d: 10 cm is the value when the radius is 5 cm. Use the reason to work out whether a radius of 6 cm gives the same length as 5 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s1.reflect: At first you almost decided the longest segment from just three measured segments. By measuring segments through the center and segments not through it separately, you formed a guess, and once you knew the reason, you could state the length in other circles too. Tell at which step your certainty became firm and what you learned then.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.prompt: There is a square box whose inside side is 12 cm. Can a round plate with a radius of 7 cm fit on the bottom of this box?
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.hint.0: Draw the plate as seen from above, and draw the segment that is its widest width.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.hint.1: Compare that width with the box's side of 12 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.o.a: It fits, because the plate's radius of 7 cm is shorter than 12 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.r.a: The radius is only the length from the middle of the plate to its edge. Look at how long the plate is across at its widest.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.o.b: It fits, because if you place it at a slant it can go in.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.r.b: The plate is round, so its widest width is the same whichever way you turn it. Think about whether turning it makes the width shorter.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.o.c: It doesn't fit, because the plate's widest width is longer than 12 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.o.d: It fits, because a round plate has no corners, so it fits well in a square box.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.r.d: Whether there are corners or not has nothing to do with the plate's widest width. Compare the box's side with the plate's width.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s2.explain: The longest segment in the plate is a segment through the center, with length 7+7=14 cm. The plate is 14 cm wide in whatever direction you place it, so it doesn't fit on the bottom of a box with a side of 12 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s3.prompt: You drew a circle with a compass opened to r cm. Find 3 different values of r so that the longest segment in this circle is at least 14 cm and at most 20 cm. r is a natural number.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s3.hint.0: Try several numbers for r and find the longest segment in that circle for each.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s3.hint.1: Check whether the length you found falls between 14 and 20, and if it doesn't, decide whether to make r larger or smaller.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s3.var.r: Length the compass is opened, r (cm)
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s3.fail.c1: Please make r a natural number that is 1 or more.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s3.ok.c2: The longest segment is at least 14 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s3.fail.c2: The longest segment is shorter than 14 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s3.ok.c3: The longest segment is at most 20 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s3.fail.c3: The longest segment is longer than 20 cm.
n-m-e3-s2-04.s.s3.explain: The longest segment in a circle is 2 times the length the compass is opened. So when r is 7, 8, 9, or 10, it is 14 cm, 16 cm, 18 cm, or 20 cm, which meets the conditions.

n-m-e3-s2-05.title: A multiplication made with 4 number cards: can the product be greater than 3000?
n-m-e3-s2-05.topic: Multiplication ((2-digit number)×(2-digit number)): making a product that is large with number cards
n-m-e3-s2-05.goal: Using four number cards, make (2-digit number)×(2-digit number) expressions yourself, compare the products, and find the rule that the product changes a lot depending on where the cards are placed.
n-m-e3-s2-05.material: There are 4 number cards. They have 2, 4, 5, and 7, one on each card. You want to use all the cards to make two 2-digit numbers and multiply them. The product changes depending on where you place the cards.
n-m-e3-s2-05.thinking.0: Making and checking expressions that meet the conditions yourself
n-m-e3-s2-05.thinking.1: Comparing the sizes of products depending on the cards' places
n-m-e3-s2-05.thinking.2: Finding what the expressions you made have in common
n-m-e3-s2-05.prereq.1: The value of the tens digit and the ones digit in a 2-digit number
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s1.prompt: Use number cards 2, 4, 5, and 7 once each to make two 2-digit numbers and multiply them. Which of the following do you think has the greatest product? Check by calculating.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s1.hint.0: Find each of the four expressions by estimating or calculating, and compare their sizes.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s1.hint.1: Make a table showing which card is in the tens place and which is in the ones place for each expression.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s1.r.b: 75×42=3150. Calculate the other expressions too and compare their sizes.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s1.r.c: 74×52=3848. Calculate the other expressions too and compare their sizes.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s1.r.d: 27×45=1215. The product changes a lot depending on which cards you put in the tens place.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s1.explain: 72×54=3888 is the greatest. 74×52=3848, 75×42=3150, 27×45=1215. Putting the two large cards in the tens place is the same, but the product changes depending on which ones-place card you pair with each.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s2.prompt: Use number cards 2, 4, 5, and 7 once each to make 2-digit numbers a and b, and make 3 different multiplication expressions where the product of a and b is greater than 3000. Count expressions with a and b swapped as the same expression.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s2.hint.0: First decide which two cards to put in the tens place, then pair the remaining cards with them in the ones place.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s2.hint.1: After making an expression, estimate the product to check whether it is over 3000, and if it isn't, move the cards and make it again.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make a and b 2-digit numbers.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s2.fail.c2: You did not use 2, 4, 5, and 7 once each.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The product is not greater than 3000.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s2.explain: The expressions with a product greater than 3000 are four: 72×54, 74×52, 72×45, and 75×42 (ones with the order swapped are the same expression). Compare side by side where the cards are placed in these expressions.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.prompt: There are only four expressions whose product is greater than 3000. What was always the same in these expressions?
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write the four expressions side by side and mark whether each card is in the tens place or the ones place.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.hint.1: Find which card's place is the same in all four expressions.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.o.a: 5 is in the tens place of one of the two numbers.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.r.a: In 45×72 and 42×75, 5 is in the ones place. Check the place of 5 in each expression.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.o.b: 7 is always in the tens place, and 2 is always in the ones place.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.o.c: 4 is in the ones place of one of the two numbers.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.r.c: In 42×75, 4 is in the tens place. Check the place of 4 in each expression.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.o.d: The tens digits of both numbers are 5 or more.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.r.d: In 42×75 and 45×72, one of the numbers has 4 in the tens place. Check the tens place in each expression.
n-m-e3-s2-05.s.s3.explain: In all four expressions 72×54, 74×52, 72×45, and 75×42, 7 is in the tens place and 2 is in the ones place. If you put the largest card in the tens place and the smallest card in the ones place, the product gets larger.

n-m-e3-s2b-01.title: Making a number between one pizza and two pizzas with fractions that have the same denominator
n-m-e3-s2b-01.topic: Fractions (improper fractions and unit fractions, size of fractions: fractions between 1 and 2)
n-m-e3-s2b-01.goal: Check with several examples when the numerator of a fraction with the same denominator makes it greater than 1 and less than 2, and tell which side the boundary fractions belong to.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.material: Seoa's group shares pizza cut into equal-sized pieces. If one pizza is divided equally into 4 pieces, one piece is 1/4 of a pizza. We write 3 pieces as 3/4 pizza and 5 pieces as 5/4 pizza. A fraction whose numerator is greater than its denominator is called an improper fraction.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.thinking.0: Deciding whether the boundary values (exactly one pizza, exactly two pizzas) fit the condition
n-m-e3-s2b-01.thinking.1: Making and checking examples in the same way for several denominators
n-m-e3-s2b-01.thinking.2: Counting the examples and checking that none is missed or overcounted
n-m-e3-s2b-01.prereq.0: Reading a fraction as whole and part (3 out of 4, etc.)
n-m-e3-s2b-01.prereq.1: Knowing improper fractions and mixed numbers
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s1.prompt: One pizza was divided equally into 4 pieces. Which of the fractions below is more than one pizza?
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s1.hint.0: Draw a picture, divide one pizza into 4 pieces, and shade the number of pieces for each choice.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the number of pieces in one pizza with the number of pieces in each choice, side by side.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s1.r.a: 3 pieces did not fill up one whole pizza, but you may have thought it was more just by looking at the number of pieces.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s1.r.b: This thought counts a fraction that is exactly the same amount as one pizza as "more than one pizza."
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s1.r.c: This thought found the case where the number of pieces is more than the number of pieces that make one pizza.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s1.r.d: This thought saw it as more even though the number of pieces is small. How many pieces make one pizza?
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s1.explain: One pizza is 4 pieces. 5 pieces is one pizza (4 pieces) and 1 piece, so it is more than one pizza. 4 pieces is exactly one pizza, and 3 pieces or 2 pieces is less than one pizza.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.prompt: Choose a denominator from 3 to 9 and make 4 different improper fractions a/b that are more than one pizza and less than two pizzas. (The denominator is b and the numerator is a.)
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a denominator and first write how many pieces one pizza is divided into.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.hint.1: Write the number of pieces in one pizza and in two pizzas, and pick a numerator between them.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.hint.2: For each fraction you made, check by comparing the numerator with the number of pieces in one pizza and in two pizzas.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The denominator is a natural number from 3 to 9.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make b a natural number from 3 to 9.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The numerator is greater than the denominator, so it is more than one pizza.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.fail.c2: It must be more than one pizza. The numerator must be greater than the denominator (the number of pieces in one pizza).
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.ok.c3: It is less than two pizzas (2b pieces).
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.fail.c3: It must be less than two pizzas. The numerator must be less than 2 times the number of pieces in one pizza.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s2.explain: If the denominator is b, one pizza is b pieces. If the numerator is greater than b and less than 2b, it meets the conditions. If the numerator equals b or 2b, it is exactly one pizza or two pizzas, so it is left out of the "more and less" condition.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s3.prompt: Among fractions with denominator 6, how many are more than one pizza and less than two pizzas in all?
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write the fractions with denominator 6 in order, with numerators from 5 to 13.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s3.hint.1: Cross out the ones that are exactly one pizza and exactly two pizzas, and count what is left.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s3.r.a: This thought counted one more fraction that is on one of the boundaries, either one pizza or two pizzas.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s3.r.b: This thought counted even the fractions equal to one pizza and two pizzas.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s3.r.c: This thought missed one fraction that meets the condition. Write the numerators in order starting from those greater than 6.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s3.r.d: This thought left out the boundaries and counted every numerator between them.
n-m-e3-s2b-01.s.s3.explain: There are 5, with numerators 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11. 6/6 is exactly one pizza and 12/6 is exactly two pizzas, so they are not included.

n-m-e3-s2b-02.title: Can we find the weight of just the tangerines from the weight measured with the box?
n-m-e3-s2b-02.topic: Capacity and weight (kg and g, subtracting weights and converting units)
n-m-e3-s2b-02.goal: Check that the weight measured with the box includes the box's own weight, so this value alone cannot determine the weight of the contents, and choose what information is needed.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.material: Jiwoo filled an empty box with tangerines and put it on a scale. The scale reads 3 kg 400 g. Jiwoo wants to know the weight of just the tangerines.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.thinking.0: Telling apart the information that is needed to solve the problem from the information that is not
n-m-e3-s2b-02.thinking.1: Checking with examples that to know one part of a whole you need the other part
n-m-e3-s2b-02.thinking.2: Converting between kg and g to calculate
n-m-e3-s2b-02.prereq.1: Reading weights that mix kg and g
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.prompt: If you could know one more thing, which one would you need to know to find the weight of just the tangerines?
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.hint.0: Write down, one by one, what is on the scale.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.hint.1: Pick each choice and ask, "If I knew only this, could I calculate the weight of just the tangerines?" and write the method.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.r.a: Think about the fact that without knowing how many tangerines there are, the weight of one tangerine does not tell you the total.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.o.b: How many tangerines there are in all
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.r.b: Think about the fact that the number alone does not tell you how much one tangerine weighs.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.o.c: The length, width, and height of the box
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.r.c: The size of the box alone does not tell you how heavy the box is.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.o.d: The weight of just the empty box
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.r.d: This thought is that if you subtract the weight of the box from the total weight, the weight of just the tangerines is left.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s1.explain: The 3 kg 400 g on the scale includes both the tangerines and the box. If you know the weight of the empty box, you can subtract it from the total to find the weight of just the tangerines. The weight of one tangerine and the number of tangerines are only useful if you know both, and the size of the box does not tell you its weight.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.prompt: Let's find out how much the tangerines could weigh when you don't know the weight of the empty box. Choose the box's weight as a g and the tangerines' weight as b g, and make three different cases where the two add up to 3 kg 400 g. Both the box and the tangerines are at least 100 g.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.hint.0: First convert 3 kg 400 g into g and write it down.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.hint.1: Choose the box's weight first, then calculate so that the rest becomes the tangerines' weight.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.hint.2: Look at how the tangerines' weight changes each time you change the box's weight.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The weights are natural numbers in g.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.fail.c1: Please write the weights as natural numbers in g.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.ok.c2: Both the box and the tangerines are at least 100 g.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Both the box and the tangerines must be at least 100 g.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.ok.c3: The sum is 3 kg 400 g (3400 g).
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.fail.c3: The two weights must add up to 3 kg 400 g. 1 kg is 1000 g.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s2.explain: If the box is light, the tangerines are heavy, and if the box is heavy, the tangerines are light. The weight of just the tangerines changes with the weight of the box, so 3 kg 400 g alone cannot decide the weight of the tangerines.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s3.prompt: Jiwoo weighed the empty box and it was 800 g. How much do the tangerines weigh by themselves?
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s3.hint.0: Write 3 kg 400 g in g only, to match the unit of 800 g.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s3.hint.1: After subtracting, group the result by 1000 g and convert it to kg.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s3.r.a: This thought added the two weights. Think about whether you should subtract the box's weight from the total.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s3.r.b: This thought subtracted the box's weight from the total weight.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s3.r.c: This thought subtracted only in the kg part and handled the g part separately. Try converting 3 kg 400 g into g.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s3.r.d: This thought used the total weight as it is, without subtracting the box's weight.
n-m-e3-s2b-02.s.s3.explain: 3 kg 400 g is 3400 g. 3400 g minus 800 g is 2600 g, which is 2 kg 600 g.

n-m-e3-s2b-03.title: If there are more pictures, were more books borrowed too?
n-m-e3-s2b-03.topic: Organizing data (picture graphs, the number one picture stands for)
n-m-e3-s2b-03.goal: When comparing different picture graphs, explain with numbers why you must look at the number each picture stands for, not just the number of pictures.
n-m-e3-s2b-03.material:
The number of books borrowed from the library over two months is shown in picture graphs.
Last month (each ● is 10 books): ● ● ● ● ●
This month (each ● is 5 books): ● ● ● ● ● ●
Seojin said, "This month has more pictures, so more books were borrowed."
n-m-e3-s2b-03.thinking.0: First checking whether the basis of comparison (the value of one picture) is the same
n-m-e3-s2b-03.thinking.1: Testing, with examples, the conditions under which a claim would be right
n-m-e3-s2b-03.thinking.2: Finding the numbers and correcting the direction of the claim
n-m-e3-s2b-03.prereq.0: How to read a picture graph (the number one picture stands for)
n-m-e3-s2b-03.prereq.1: Multiplying with 2-digit numbers and comparing large numbers
n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s1.prompt: To find out whether Seojin is right, what should you look at first in the two graphs?
n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s1.hint.0: Read aloud the notes written beside the two graphs, and find what is the same and what is different.
n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s1.hint.1: Tell how you could find out how many books there are when there are 4 pictures and when there are 6 pictures.
n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s1.o.a: Whether the two months have the same number of days
n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s1.r.a: The number of days could affect the number of books, but that is a different matter from reading the graph. Look first at the value the pictures stand for.
n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s1.o.b: Whether the pictures in the two graphs are drawn the same size
n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s1.r.b: You must read the number the pictures stand for, not the size of the pictures.
n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s1.o.c: How many more pictures one graph has than the other
n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s1.r.c: The difference in the number of pictures alone does not tell you the difference in the number of books.

n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s1.explain: A picture graph sets the number that one picture stands for and shows data with the number of pictures. If the number one picture stands for differs between the two graphs, you cannot compare them by the number of pictures alone.

n-m-e3-s2b-03.s.s3.prompt: Tell Seojin. In the real graphs (each ● this month is 5 books), find and write the number of books for the two months to show which month had more books borrowed, and also write why you can't compare using only the number of pictures.

n-m-e3-s2b-04.title: What is strange in Hayun's calculation of combining two cups of water?
n-m-e3-s2b-04.topic: Capacity and weight (adding capacities: L and mL, regrouping)
n-m-e3-s2b-04.goal: In an addition mixing L and mL, find in the calculation steps that when the sum of mL is 1000 mL or more it must be carried to L, fix it, and make an example where carrying happens.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.material: Hayun poured 1 L 700 mL of juice and 2 L 600 mL of water into a big container. She calculated the amount in the container like this.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.thinking.0: Checking the calculation line by line
n-m-e3-s2b-04.thinking.1: Reasoning about where to move a value when changing units
n-m-e3-s2b-04.thinking.2: Making cases where carrying happens yourself
n-m-e3-s2b-04.prereq.1: How to add L and mL separately
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one line in Hayun's calculation that is strange.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s1.hint.0: Check one by one whether each line follows from the result of the line before it.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s1.hint.1: After splitting 1300 mL into L and mL, follow where the resulting L should be used.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s1.line.0: Adding the L parts gives 1 L + 2 L = 3 L.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s1.line.1: Adding the mL parts gives 700 mL + 600 mL = 1300 mL.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s1.line.3: So the big container holds 3 L 300 mL.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 to 3 are all correct. 1300 mL, the sum of 700 mL and 600 mL, can be split into 1 L and 300 mL, but line 4 is wrong because it leaves out adding that 1 L to the 3 L from adding the L parts. The correct sum is 4 L 300 mL.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.prompt: Let's make additions where carrying happens. Choose a mL of water in the first cup and b mL of water in the second cup so that the sum is at least 4000 mL and less than 5000 mL, and when you split the water in the two cups into L and mL, adding the mL parts gives 1000 mL or more. Make two different pairs.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.hint.0: Split a and b each into "L and mL" and write them.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.hint.1: Add the two mL parts and check whether they are over 1000.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.hint.2: Look at how the sum of the L parts and the sum of the mL parts go into the total.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.ok.c1: The amounts of water are natural numbers in mL.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.fail.c1: Please write the amounts of water as natural numbers in mL.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum is at least 4000 mL and less than 5000 mL.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The total of the two cups must be at least 4000 mL and less than 5000 mL.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.ok.c3: Adding the mL parts gives 1000 mL or more, so it is carried to L.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.fail.c3: When a and b are split into L and mL, the sum of the mL parts (the part beyond 1000 mL) must be 1000 mL or more.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s2.explain: If the mL parts are small, as with 3000 mL and 400 mL, no carrying is needed. For 1700 mL and 2600 mL, the mL parts are 700 and 600, so their sum is 1300 mL, and 1000 mL must be carried to 1 L.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s3.prompt: How much is 1 L 700 mL + 2 L 600 mL? Choose the best way to show it.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s3.hint.0: Convert both amounts to mL and add, then show the result in L and mL again.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s3.hint.1: Compare it with the result of adding after splitting into L and mL.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s3.r.a: This thought changed 1300 mL into 1 L 300 mL but then did not add that 1 L.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s3.r.b: This thought added the mL sum to the L side one more time without converting it to L.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s3.r.c: This thought added the 1 L from the mL sum to the L side.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s3.r.d: This thought left the mL sum of 1300 mL as it is, without converting it to L.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s3.explain: Adding the 1 L carried from 1300 mL to 3 L, the sum of 1 L and 2 L, gives 4 L, and the remaining mL is 300 mL. So the sum is 4 L 300 mL.
n-m-e3-s2b-04.s.s3.acc.0: 3 L 1300 mL is the same amount as 4 L 300 mL. But when the mL part goes over 1000 mL, the correct way to write it is to change it to 1 L and write 4 L 300 mL.

n-m-e3-s2b-05.title: Two fraction cards: which one is greater?
n-m-e3-s2b-05.topic: Fractions (mixed numbers and improper fractions, comparing fractions with the same denominator)
n-m-e3-s2b-05.goal: Follow new information to fix where the method of comparing only numerators works and where it fails for fractions with the same denominator, and choose a way to compare mixed numbers and improper fractions.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.material: Hajun and Seoa play a game where they draw fraction cards and the greater one wins. The cards have fractions written like 3/4 and fractions with a whole number and a fraction together like 2 1/4. Hajun first thought of one rule. Each time a new card comes out, think about whether that rule is right.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.thinking.0: Pointing out how far a correct rule can be used
n-m-e3-s2b-05.thinking.1: Comparing by changing the form (mixed numbers and improper fractions)
n-m-e3-s2b-05.thinking.2: Fixing my thinking according to new information
n-m-e3-s2b-05.prereq.0: Knowing mixed numbers and improper fractions
n-m-e3-s2b-05.prereq.1: Comparing proper fractions with the same denominator
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose how your thinking changes each time a new card comes out.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first write, "If I use Hajun's rule, what happens with this card?"
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.hint.1: Draw a picture or change to improper fractions and compare with the result of the rule.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.0.info: One pizza was divided equally into 4 pieces. Card 가 is 3/4 and card 나 is 5/4. Hajun says, "The denominators are the same, so the one with the greater numerator is greater."
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.0.ask: What do you think of what Hajun says?
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.0.after: If the denominators are the same, each piece is the same size, so the one with more pieces (the numerator) is the greater fraction.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.0.o.a: The denominators are the same, so the two fractions are the same size.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.0.r.a: If the denominators are the same, only the size of each piece is the same, and the number of pieces is different.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.0.o.b: The pieces are the same size, so 5/4, which has more pieces, is greater.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.0.o.c: If there are more pieces, the pieces get smaller, so 5/4 is smaller.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Pieces get smaller when the denominator gets larger. Here the denominators are the same and only the number of pieces (the numerator) is different.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.0.o.d: You can only tell which is greater by drawing a picture.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.0.r.d: A picture helps, but if you use the fact that the pieces are the same size, you can tell without a picture.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.1.info: Card 다 is 2 1/4 (2 and 1 fourth) and card 라 is 7/4. Using the same method, Hajun says, "The numerator of 2 1/4 is 1 and the numerator of 7/4 is 7, so card 라 is greater."
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.1.after: The numerator 1 in 2 1/4 is the number of leftover pieces apart from the two pizzas. If you compare only the numerators, you leave out the whole number 2 in front.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The denominators are the same, so this time too you only need to look at the numerators.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Think about the fact that the numerator 1 in a mixed number is just the number of pieces left after the whole number 2.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Mixed numbers are smaller than improper fractions, so card 라 is greater.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.1.r.b: There is no such rule between mixed numbers and improper fractions. The size depends on the numbers.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.1.o.c: 2 1/4 also has the whole number 2, so you have to consider that too.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Both are some fourths, so they are the same size.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.1.r.d: Having the same denominator does not mean the two numbers are equal.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.2.info: Hajun drew 7/4 as a picture. 4 pieces make one pizza and 3 pieces are left. Now let's work out which is greater, 2 1/4 or 7/4.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which of the two cards is greater, and how would be a good way to compare them?
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.2.after: 7/4 is one pizza and 3 pieces, and 2 1/4 is two pizzas and 1 piece, so card 다 is greater. Changing to 9/4 and 7/4 to compare gives the same result.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Card 라 is greater, because the numerator 7 is greater than 1.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This thought used the numerator comparison that was wrong in the previous step.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.2.o.b: They are equal, because both have denominator 4.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Having the same denominator is different from being the same size.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.2.o.c: They can't be compared, because mixed numbers and improper fractions are different kinds.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Even if they are different kinds, you can compare them if you change them to the same form.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Card 다 is greater. Change both to the same form and compare.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.3.info: This time the cards are card 마, 3 2/5, and card 바, 3 4/5.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.3.ask: How would be a good way to compare this time?
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.3.after: If the whole number parts are the same, you only need to compare the fraction parts. If the whole number parts are different, the one with the greater whole number part is greater.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.3.o.a: The whole number parts are the same, so compare the fraction parts 2/5 and 4/5.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.3.o.b: The whole number parts are the same, so the two cards are the same size.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.3.r.b: This thought missed that the fraction parts are different.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.3.o.c: Mixed numbers can be compared only after being changed to improper fractions.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.3.r.c: You can change them to improper fractions, but you don't have to.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.3.o.d: Always drop the whole number part and look only at the fraction part.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.st.3.r.d: This time the answer is right, but it fails when the whole number parts are different, like 3 2/5 and 2 4/5. It is a method you can use only when the whole number parts are the same.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s1.reflect: The first rule was right when comparing proper fractions or improper fractions with the same denominator. When mixed numbers came up, looking only at the numerator was wrong because it left out the whole number part. Changing to the same form solved it, and for mixed numbers with the same whole number part, comparing only the fraction parts worked. Tell how far the rule is right.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s2.prompt: Among mixed numbers with denominator 4, make three different ones that are greater than 7/4. The whole number part is w and the fraction part is n/4. (n is one of 1, 2, or 3.)
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s2.hint.0: Choose a mixed number and rewrite it as some fourths (an improper fraction).
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the numerator of that improper fraction with 7.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s2.var.n: Numerator of the fraction part n
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s2.ok.c1: w and n are natural numbers.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make w a natural number that is 1 or more, and n a natural number.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The fraction part is a proper fraction (n is 1, 2, or 3).
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s2.fail.c3: It must be a number greater than 7/4. One pizza is 4 pieces, so change it to the total number of pieces and compare.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s2.explain: 1 3/4 is equal to 7/4, and to be greater than that, the whole number part must be 2 or more. 1 1/4 and 1 2/4, which are less than 1 3/4, are less than 7/4.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.prompt: Card 사 is 3 1/5 and card 아 is 13/5. How is it right to compare them, and which card is greater?
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.hint.0: Apply Hajun's first rule (looking only at numerators) to these two cards. Compare that result with the result from drawing a picture.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.hint.1: Test whether you can show each of the two cards as some fifths.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.o.a: Card 아 is greater, because the numerator 13 is greater than 1.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.r.a: The numerator 1 in a mixed number is just the number of pieces left after the whole number 3. This is the method that was wrong in the previous step.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.o.b: They are equal, because both have denominator 5.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.r.b: Having the same denominator is different from being the same size.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.o.c: Card 사 is greater. Changing 3 1/5 to 16/5 gives a numerator greater than 13/5's.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.o.d: They can't be compared, because mixed numbers and improper fractions are different kinds.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.r.d: Even if they are different kinds, you can compare them if you change them to the same form.
n-m-e3-s2b-05.s.s3.explain: 3 1/5, when one pizza is 5 pieces, is 3 pizzas and 1 piece, so it is 16 pieces. 13/5 is 13 pieces. Changing to the same form and comparing 16/5 and 13/5, card 사 is greater. Comparing only the numerators 1 and 13 as they are is wrong.
